[MUQATIL:22:11-12/r6] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The idol worshipper invokes what cannot harm him in this world if neglected or benefit him in the Hereafter if worshipped; this is far-reaching misguidance.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p357/r2] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | holds | The object invoked besides God is an idol that can neither harm nor benefit, and this is distant error.
[FARRA:v2p217/r2] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | The object of يدعو من دون الله is idols.
[TAB-FULL:v16p476/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | When a person worshipping God precariously meets a trial and apostatizes, he calls on idols that cannot harm him if neglected in this life or benefit him in the next; this is a remote departure from God's path.
[TAB-FULL:v16p476/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن زيد | reports | Ibn Zayd glosses the passage as a person disbelieving after having believed.
[ZAJJAJ:v3p414#2/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The one invoked besides God is an idol that neither hears nor sees nor benefits nor harms.
[NAHHAS:v3p88/r3] NAHHAS, d. 338 · الفراء | reports | He glosses ḥarf as the long edge or side.
[SULAMI:v2p19#2/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · السياري | reports | If God decrees someone's humiliation from the beginning, no one can honor him; the garment of Truth remains unchanged forever.
[SULAMI:v2p19/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · ابن عطاء | reports | Whoever leans on anything besides the Real relies on what harms rather than benefits; whoever relies on God relies on the source of everything.
[THALABI:v7p9#2/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Calling on anything besides God is useless: it can neither harm when disobeyed nor benefit when obeyed, and this is far misguidance.
[THALABI:v7p9#2/r11] THALABI, d. 427 · بعض النحاة | reports | Some grammarians treat the lām in يدعو لمن as an extra particle; Ibn Masud's reading omits it.
[THALABI:v7p9#2/r12] THALABI, d. 427 · الفراء والزجاج | reports | They say the lām is displaced later in the sentence, yielding the sense that he invokes one whose harm is nearer than his benefit.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v15p289/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The person returning to unbelief worships things besides God, namely stones, which neither harm him if he does not worship them nor benefit him if he obeys them; this is far from truth and right guidance.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:22:8-12/r6] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | The idols invoked apart from God neither harm their worshippers when disobeyed nor benefit them when obeyed; relying on them is distant misguidance.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p307/r1] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | rejects | Jurjānī rejects locating compositional thought in isolated wording: either meanings receive no thought or words are thought about apart from understood meanings, both implausible.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p307/r2] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | The speaker orders meanings before their verbal signs; words serve meanings, so their order follows the author’s thought rather than generating it for the hearer.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p307/r3] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | rejects | A listener hears words before grasping meanings, but that cannot show that meanings are ordered from words; analysis must consider the composing speaker, not the listener.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p307/r4] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | A Bedouin need not know formal grammatical labels to compose correctly, just as early scholars knew theological truths without later technical terms; understanding the distinctions is what matters.
[JURJANI-DALAIL:v1p307/r5] JURJANI-DALAIL, d. 471 · author | holds | A Bedouin’s objection to the muezzin’s accusative “Muhammadan” by asking “what did he do?” shows intuitive recognition that the utterance lacked a predicate.
[JISHUMI:v7p4920/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Ashir means companion, spouse, or one who associates with another.
[JISHUMI:v7p4922/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الزجاج | reports | Grammatically, “that” is an object of “calls” and functions like a relative pronoun; the phrase about the one whose harm is nearer begins a new clause, or “that” may be nominative with “a wretched protector” as its predicate.
[JISHUMI:v7p4922/r10] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | The powerless objects are idols; alternatively, obedience to them brings no benefit and disobedience brings no harm. The worshipper turns to idols or leaders whose harm is nearer than their benefit.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p369/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | The idol neither harms the worshipper if he abandons its worship nor benefits him if he worships it; this is far from truth and right guidance.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p110/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The objects called upon are idols; yadʿu can mean worshipping them or invoking them in distress.
[TABRISI:22:11-15#2/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj supplies three syntactic possibilities for يدعو لمن ضره: the lām may be a postponed emphatic particle, يدعو may be circumstantial with an implied object, or ذلك may be a relative pronoun whose clause is its object.
[TABRISI:22:11-15#2/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | The author explains that يدعو may mean ‘calls out/says’ or ‘names’; in the latter case the cited Ibn Ahmar verse shows a thing being called by a name.
[TABRISI:22:11-15#2/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · عنترة | reports | Antara's line in which warriors call to him illustrates يدعو in the sense of calling or addressing someone.
[TABRISI:22:11-15/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | The syntax of لمن ضره is disputed: one account fronts an emphatic oath lām and supplies an implicit pronoun with يدعو; other analyses construe the phrase as a new subject and predicate or as the object of يدعو.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v5p411/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The apostate worships what neither harms him if he does not worship it nor benefits him if he obeys it; this is remote misguidance, far from the truth.
[RAZI-FULL:v23p13/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | The one who calls on something besides God that neither harms nor benefits is most likely a polytheist worshipping idols, which makes the passage unlikely to concern a Jew.
[RAZI-FULL:v23p13/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Razi says the passage likely concerns polytheists who attached themselves to the Messenger hypocritically.
[QURTUBI-FULL:22:12/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The verse describes someone reverting to disbelief and worshipping an idol that can neither harm nor benefit him.
[QURTUBI-FULL:22:12/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ glosses al-ḍalāl al-baʿīd as long error.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:22:12/r1] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | They worship an inert thing besides God that can neither harm nor benefit; this is far error from the goal, like wandering astray in the wilderness.
[NASAFI-FULL:v3p97#5/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | After apostasy, the idol neither harms if left unserved nor benefits if worshipped; this is far error.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p402/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Those who invoke idols and rivals seek help, victory, and provision from things that neither harm nor benefit; their harm in this world is nearer than any benefit, and in the next it is certain.
[BIQAI-FULL:v5p137#2/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Everything other than God is beneath the rank of the one possessing all perfection; worship is merited by chosen action, not by compelled natural behavior.
[BIQAI-FULL:v5p137#2/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The repeated 'what' makes clear that the idol neither causes any harm nor can block benefit, and does not benefit or avert harm; blame does not require absence of both qualities together.
[BIQAI-FULL:v5p137#2/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Calling on a powerless object is gross folly and remote misguidance: leaving its worship cannot stop God's beneficence, and worship cannot secure benefit from it or avert harm.
[BIQAI-FULL:v5p137/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The unstable worshipper then invokes besides God what can neither harm nor benefit, truly relying on something other than God and abandoning the exclusive plea for divine help. | mentions 1:5
[DURR-FULL:v6p15/r2] DURR-FULL, d. 911 · السدي | reports | The idol cannot harm one who disobeys it or benefit one who obeys; its harm comes in the afterlife, and it is a bad protector.
[BURSEVI:v6p7#3/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The clause resumes the account of the apostate polytheist's great loss: he worships something besides God.
[BURSEVI:v6p7#3/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The object worshipped can neither harm the worshipper if left alone nor benefit him when worshipped; the repeated ما underscores that it is an inert object.
[BURSEVI:v6p7#3/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Calling this worship remote misguidance is a metaphor for a traveler lost in wilderness whose route grows longer and farther from the path.
[ALUSI-FULL:v17p124#3/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | The clause about worshipping other than God may be a new sentence exposing another fault, explaining the scale of the loss, or a circumstantial clause from the person who turned away, with the preceding material parenthetical.
[ALUSI-FULL:v17p124#3/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | These readings make the verse unlikely to describe a Jew, since Jews do not worship idols even though they took rabbis and monks as lords.
[ALUSI-FULL:v17p124#3/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The objects are apparently idols; supplication means worshipping, beyond God, what cannot harm if left unserved or benefit if worshipped.
[ALUSI-FULL:v17p124#3/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Alternatively, supplication means calling upon a lifeless thing to rescue the caller from affliction, although it cannot harm or benefit; repeating ma indicates an inanimate object.

d. 1270 · author | holds | Far error is a metaphor for wandering far into a wilderness, away from the right path.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p30/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The phrase that the count is ten complete may seem obvious, but it prevents a mistaken reading that only seven are meant on returning. | mentions 2:196
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p30/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | He closes with an unattributed line comparing successive manifestations to stars, each setting star giving way to others.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p30/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | Al-Ālūsī rejects the claim that ʿUthmān acknowledged Qur'anic grammatical errors: it is implausible that the Companions collectively wrote, missed, and left such errors uncorrected; he calls the report weak, disrupted, and disconnected.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p30/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · عبد الله بن عبد الأعلى | reports | A report says that after the codex was completed, ʿUthmān praised the work and noticed something to be corrected by their tongues; al-Ālūsī says this means they later corrected dialectal forms at review.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p30/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · عائشة | reports | In a report al-Ālūsī calls sound on the conditions of the two Ṣaḥīḥs, ʿĀʾisha says scribes erred in writing the forms inn hādhāni, al-muqīmīn, and al-ṣābiʾūn. | mentions 20:63, 4:162, 5:69
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p30/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Al-Ālūsī explains ʿĀʾisha's claim as choosing a less suitable dialect among the seven readings when unifying the community, not writing an impermissible error into the Qur'an. | mentions 20:63, 4:162, 5:69
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p30/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Saʿīd ibn Jubayr read al-muqīmīn al-ṣalāh and called it a scribe's grammatical error; al-Ālūsī says laḥn can mean language or reading, and notes another reading and the grammarians' analyses. | mentions 4:162
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p30/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | On the no-contradiction account, the whole Qur'an is miraculous as a complete work, so sound sermons or poetry and the shortness of individual sūras do not disprove it.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p30/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Scholars also cite the Qur'an's awe, the reciter's growing love despite repetition, its lasting presence, and God's promise to preserve it as features of its excellence.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p30/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Al-Ālūsī's own view is that the whole Qur'an, including its shortest sūra, is miraculous in its order, eloquence, unseen reports, rational accord, and subtle meaning; some aspects may be hidden while others suffice.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v17p215/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The clause about invoking other than God is circumstantial to the subject of انقلب in 22:11. | mentions 22:11
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v17p215/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Mentioning harm before benefit hints that the wavering person abandons Islam to escape perceived harm, imagining Islam caused it and idols are angry; the following clause mocks this mistaken appeal.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v17p215/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The idols neither cause harm nor bring benefit, so asking them to remove distress and secure advantage is a mistake.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v17p215/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | ذلك points to the invocation; its demonstrative, separating pronoun, and restriction work as in 22:11, while البعيد marks idolatry as an extreme degree of error because the objects have no utility. | mentions 22:11
[TABATABAI:22:11-15/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | An idol cannot harm or benefit because it lacks awareness and will; the harm and loss its worshipper suffers comes from the worshipper's own act.
[ASAD-NOTES:22:12#n11/r1] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | People who do not commit fully to their professed faith may assign decisive influence over destiny to real or imagined forces, thereby granting them divine qualities.
[ASAD-NOTES:22:12#n12/r1] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · author | holds | The literal wording is “this, this is the far-away straying”; Asad refers to his explanation of this paraphrase at 14:18. | mentions 14:18
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p179/r1] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | The verb ‘invoke’ includes praying, pleading, beseeching, and seeking help or mercy; assigning another being authority to harm or benefit is polytheism, since only God controls this and all reliance should be on Him.
[ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-5-english:p179/r2] ISLAHI-TADABBUR · author | holds | The parable in 22:73 shows the extreme error of seeking refuge with beings unable even to create a fly or recover what it steals; fleeing God’s trial thus ends in Hell. | mentions 22:73
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:22:11/r3] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · müfessirler | reports | Commentators offer linguistic explanations for the apparent difference between verse 12’s beings that can neither harm nor benefit and verse 13’s beings whose harm is nearer than their benefit.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:22:11/r5] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · bir yorum | reports | Another interpretation keeps the reference to idols: idols themselves neither help nor harm, but worshipping them causes harm by costing their devotees the afterlife.
[KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:22:11/r7] KURANYOLU-TEFSIR · author | holds | Even after turning from God, these people cannot stop worshipping and supplicating; they turn to beings that are useless or likely to harm them.
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p705/r1] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT · author | holds | The surrounding الحج passage continues describing false deities and emphasizes their falsity, linking 22:12 with further condemnations of worshipping other than God. | mentions 22:13, 22:31, 22:71, 22:73
[SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p705/r2] SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT · author | holds | Samarrāʾī counts the pronoun huwa 13 times in al-Ḥajj and 7 in Luqmān, including the pronoun of separation 8 versus 3 times, to explain its heavier stylistic presence here.
[STUDYQURAN:22:12/r1] STUDYQURAN · author | reports | Commentators usually understand these verses as referring to idols and false gods, often described as neither harming nor benefiting their worshippers. | mentions 6:71, 10:18, 10:106, 20:89, 21:66, 25:55, 26:73
[STUDYQURAN:22:intro/r1] STUDYQURAN · IK | reports | One dating view holds that the surah is Madinan except verses 52–55, which are Makkan.
[STUDYQURAN:22:intro/r2] STUDYQURAN · Q | reports | Another dating view holds that the surah is Makkan except verses 19–22, which are Madinan.
[STUDYQURAN:22:intro/r3] STUDYQURAN · Q | reports | Most authorities regard the surah as containing both Makkan and Madinan verses.
[STUDYQURAN:22:intro/r4] STUDYQURAN · Q | reports | A tradition calls the surah remarkable because it came at night and by day, on journeys and at home, in war and peace, and includes abrogating and abrogated as well as clear and allegorical verses.
[STUDYQURAN:22:intro/r7] STUDYQURAN · author | holds | The passage contrasts the misguided and righteous through a garden parable and their respective afterlife reward or punishment.

<<end of notes>>
